text.tspan: Functional fingerprinting refers to an ensemble of methods, like Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC), that try to identify a characteristic
pattern of Functional Connectivity (FC) in subjects that share one or several features (e.g. cognitive traits, symptoms1).
FC fluctuations reflect autonomous processes, such as breathing and cardiac cycles, and some sources of noise show an idiosyncratic structure2.
Certain effects of noise on fingerprinting are known in few sessions3, but not in dense sampled data.
This study assessed the role of noise regression, atlas coarseness and number of independent sessions on functional fingerprinting.
Ten healthy subjects (24-40yrs) underwent 10-minute resting-state BOLD
multi-echo sequence ten times every seven days at the same time of the day.
Anatomical and functional data were minimally preprocessed4. Peak detection for
PPG and chest belt signals was run automatically, then manually corrected, with
peakdet5. Respiratory variance per time (RVT), heart rate variability
(HRV), and 16 RETROICOR regressors were computed with phys2denoise. RVT
and HRV were convolved with respiratory6 and cardiac7 response function.

tspan.tspan: than group-level FC variability indicates subject distinctiveness. We computed ICC
topographical distribution of most stable edges
for each denoising approach, summing all maps.

text.tspan: ICC scores were higher compared to previous findings10 (mean = 0.32-0.52).
Dense-sampling definitely influences fingerprinting, with the highest ICC
achieved when considering 6 sessions, regardless of noise correction.
Tissue-denoised and physiologically-denoised data seem to provide the most
stable and reliable results across time and atlases.
Coarser parcellations benefit more from physiological noise regression in terms of
ICC, but average ICC trends are the same across atlases.
ICC is generally higher within Somatomotor (SMT) and Dorsal Attention (DA)
networks, but when tissue- and physiological denoising highest ICC scores are found in
the default mode network (DMN) and fronto-parietal network (FPN).
